newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco deal faces uncertain future in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco deal faces uncertain future in Congress.

text.p: A historic agreement between tobacco companies and states requires complex legislation from a fractious Congress where lawmakers on both sides of the issue will try to pick it apart.

Initial reaction from Congress to the $368.5 billion agreement was cautious, with Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich saying they were awaiting details.
They and others of the majority Republicans made clear that a deal negotiated outside the confines of Congress would be regarded as a set of recommendations, not etched in stone.

"The constitution does not have any provision for the Congress to delegate (decision-making) to a private group in a secret meeting," Gingrich said of the settlement agreement among the tobacco companies and 40 states suing them.
"We'll be glad to look at what they think their settlement is... Whether or not that becomes law will be a function of the congressional committees, the hearing process," he said.

The likely scenario is a tug of war, with tobacco foes trying to toughen up the deal, and lawmakers from tobacco-producing states trying to ensure the industry does not lose anything more than agreed at the bargaining table, Congressional sources said.

Some of the harshest critics of the industry, including California Democratic Rep. Henry Waxman and New Jersey Democratic Sen. Frank Lautenberg, said the accord was a "positive first step" but they might try to make it tougher.
"We've got to go in there with an editing pencil, not a rubber stamp," said Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat.

Representatives of states that grow or manufacture tobacco, like North Carolina Republican Sen. Jesse Helms or House Commerce committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, have had little to say about the accord so far.
"Anything this important deserves a full, fair and public review by the Congress," Bliley said in a statement.

One of the few tobacco-state senators to be openly dubious was Kentucky Democrat Wendell Ford, also one of the few lawmakers who smokes in public. "I couldn't vote for something if it didn't help the (tobacco) farmers," he said recently.

It would be a cumbersome undertaking for Congress to consider the sweeping deal. Any tobacco legislation translated from the agreement could touch on health policy, liability, farming and the Food and Drug Administration. Several House and Senate comittees could have a piece of it.

If the White House and the Republican Congressional leadership sign off on the deal, it could move quickly as a relatively intact package. But nobody is rushing ahead on something so costly, complex and politically sensitive.

Lawmakers and Congressional staff expect the agreement to get divided up among committees and subcommittees for consideration, each of which could hold prolonged hearings and come up with its own version of portions of a plan.

That sets up jurisdictional battles and also means there are more opportunities to change or stall a bill as it passes through more legislative hands and becomes a better target for lobbyists and advocacy groups.
Traditionally, the well-heeled tobacco lobby has been powerful on Capitol Hill, but anti-smoking activists see the tide turning because of public opinion and high-profile lawsuits.

Congressional sources do not expect tobacco to dominate their agenda immediately. President Bill Clinton wants to hear the views of the leading public health experts and a special panel within his administration before he passes judgment on the complicated deal.
Lott said on Thursday that the Congressional agenda was so packed any agreement probably could not be considered until the autumn.
